statement: On 10 August 2024, as described in the journal's three retraction notices (read in full on the publisher's pages), Psychopharmacology retracted three analyses from the sponsor's phase 2 programme of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD, published online in 2019 and 2020: a pooled analysis of six phase 2 trials that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials, a pooled long-term follow-up of six phase 2 trials, and an analysis of how stopping medicines classified as reuptake inhibitors affected treatment response. The editors state that they had been informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at one study site (MP4), that the authors confirmed knowing of these violations when they submitted but had neither disclosed them to the journal nor removed that site's data, and that a potential competing interest was not fully declared (authors affiliated with MAPS or its wholly owned subsidiary MAPS PBC; the notices state that MAPS fully funded and provided the MDMA used and that MAPS PBC organised the trial). Of the authors who responded to the publisher, most disagreed with the retractions (6 of 8, 4 of 5 and 3 of 4). The notices do not describe the violations, say when the editors were informed or how much of the analysed data came from the site, and do not mention the phase 3 trials; the BMJ, citing a New York Times report and a 2019 statement by MAPS, says reports suggest that an investigator at one study site had an unethical sexual relationship with a trial participant. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: In August 2024 a journal withdrew three earlier studies from the research programme behind the MDMA therapy trials. It said the authors knew of serious rule-breaking at one study site and did not tell it, and had not fully declared their ties to the sponsor. Most of the authors who answered the journal disagreed. The journal did not say what the rule-breaking was.
population: Published analyses of the sponsor's (MAPS) phase 2 trials of MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD
exposure: Three retraction notices issued by Psychopharmacology on 10 August 2024
outcome: The fact of the retractions, the journal's stated grounds and the authors' recorded positions
magnitude: Not a quantity. Three retraction notices, published online on 10 August 2024 (Psychopharmacology 241, pp. 2403, 2405 and 2407; November 2024 issue), for articles published online on 7 May 2019 (Mithoefer et al.), 4 June 2020 (Jerome et al.) and 21 November 2020 (Feduccia et al.). Authors' positions: Mithoefer et al., 1 agrees with the retraction but not its wording, 6 disagree, 1 neither agrees nor disagrees, 2 did not respond; Jerome et al., 1 agrees but not with the wording, 4 disagree, 3 did not respond; Feduccia et al., 1 agrees but not with the wording, 3 disagree.

evidence.extracted: Retraction note published 10 August 2024 for the pooled analysis of six phase 2 randomized trials that set out the design and rationale for the phase 3 trials (published online 7 May 2019). Grounds: the editors were informed of protocol violations amounting to unethical conduct at the MP4 study site by researchers associated with the project; the authors confirmed they knew of these at submission but neither disclosed them nor removed that site's data; a potential competing interest was not fully declared (several authors affiliated with MAPS or its wholly owned subsidiary MAPS PBC; MAPS fully funded the work and provided the MDMA, MAPS PBC organised the trial). One author agrees with the retraction but not its wording, six disagree, one neither agrees nor disagrees and two did not respond.

evidence.extracted: The notices did not detail the violations; reports (ref 4, a New York Times article of 12 August 2024; ref 5, a 2019 MAPS statement announcing an ethical violation by former MAPS-sponsored investigators) suggest that a trial investigator at one study site had an unethical sexual relationship with a trial participant; in a 2018 lawsuit settled out of court the participant said she had been sexually assaulted, and the investigator said it was consensual (ref 6, a CBC report).

risk_of_bias.note: The journal's own notices, read in full, with matching Crossref update links.

inconsistency.note: The three notices give the same grounds.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claims are never upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: A description of documented events, rated as a description (METHODS §6.3): it starts low and is never upgraded. The three notices are the journal's own record of its decision, its stated grounds and the authors' positions, read in full on the publisher's pages, with Crossref update-to and updated-by links that match (study cards); no domain is rated down. What the violations were rests on the BMJ's second-hand account, given as such and not rated. Status single study: three notices from one journal, issued together on the same grounds.
